summary: 30-min follow-up on the Feb 2nd incident where high sequence-length traffic triggered a KV-cache eviction bug and autoscaler limit, causing inference queue buildup. We reviewed root cause, confirmed hotfixs that were deployed, and agreed on mitigations: autoscaler thresholds, queue-depth alerts, fallback model policy, and a temporary dedicated capacity pilot. Next steps include sharing RCA/logs, bench run, and runbook updates.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-02-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Aegis SRE), Tom Reynolds (Aegis Head of MLOps), Lisa Chen (Aegis Product)
---
[00:00] Alex Martinez: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this tight, 45-ish minutes follow up on the feb 2 incident, quick recap then root cause and next steps. samir do you wanna kick off the technical summary?
[00:22] Samir Patel: yeah thanks alex. So quick refresher, on feb 2 around 13:24 UTC you saw a spike in long-sequence requests to the fraud model, sequences that were 8k to 12k tokens. Those triggered an unexpected kv-cache eviction pattern - our cache eviction logic didn't account for mixed sequence lengths and we had a cascade: big sequences cause larger kv page allocations, which pushed other models' KV out, which then produced a high miss rate, then the runtime tried to re-populate and gpu memory usage spiked. Autoscaler tried to spin up extra nodes but hit the account burst limit and also a policy mismatch where the fallback routing wasn't considered because model variant tags didn't match the policy. net result: request queue backlog, timeouts and 20-30 minute increased latencies for some endpoints.
[01:18] Priya Nair: yep that matches what we saw - our dashboards showed queue depth to 120 and p95 from 220ms to 4.1s, some 500s for about 12 minutes. our on-call pager fired, we switched traffic to the smaller ensemble but some jobs were pinned to the primary model on the app side which slowed rollback.
[01:40] Tom Reynolds: to add, our constraint was that we have strict burst limits on the account, we didn't want to blow past that without approval, so the autoscaler aborting made sense but we needed a graceful fallback instead.
[01:57] Alex Martinez: got it. samir, what was the immediate mitigation you pushed during the incident?
[02:05] Samir Patel: we deployed a hotfix to KV eviction logic to avoid mass-invalidations for large sequences, and temporarily lowered the default max sequence length acceptance so requests above 6k tokens were truncated at the gateway. also we updated the fallback routing to allow model-variant fallback even when tag mismatch - that prevented further backlog. these were quick patches to stop the bleeding.
[02:38] Lisa Chen: the truncation helped but we saw degraded quality for a subset of requests, so prods team was hesitant about it as a long term solution.
[02:48] Samir Patel: totally, truncation is a stop gap. long term we'd prefer either use dedicated capacity or pre-warmed large-sequence variants for that workload.
[03:01] Priya Nair: how did the KV bug slip through? did we have tests for mixed-length sequences?
[03:07] Samir Patel: we have unit tests for eviction policies but not an integration test that simulates mixed long/short sequences at scale. that's on us. we'll add a regression test to the eval harness and run a bench with mixed seq lengths.
[03:25] Alex Martinez: ok let's talk root cause at a high level, then mitigations and ops changes. Root cause chain: 1) sudden traffic pattern with many long sequences; 2) KV eviction misbehavior for mixed lengths; 3) autoscaler policy + account burst limit prevented capacity from appearing; 4) fallback/matching policy didn't trigger for pinned requests.
[03:48] Tom Reynolds: that aligns. i want to call out that our client SDK pins model names per route, which made the fallback not kick in. we'll change routing to allow a fallback alias in the SDK.
[04:02] Lisa Chen: ok. also curious about alerts - queue depth alert didn't fire?
[04:08] Priya Nair: it did but the alert threshold was 100 and we were hitting 120 - it fired but the escalation didn't go to the ML on-call, it went to infra and there was some page handoff friction.
[04:21] Alex Martinez: so we need clearer alert routing and maybe a lower threshold for queue depth for that route.
[04:27] Samir Patel: agreed. We'll propose new alert rules: queue depth at 60 for critical models, p95 latency 1s, and automatic ticket creation to ML on-call.
[04:40] Priya Nair: that sounds good. also we want an SLA-based protection: if latency >X for >Y minutes, auto-burst to dedicated capacity even if account limit is near - with a budget guard to avoid runaway cost.
[04:55] Samir Patel: we can propose a policy for that - automatic funding hold or a user-confirmable temporary capacity. we need to align with you on acceptable budget thresholds.
[05:07] Tom Reynolds: we can allow an emergency budget of $5k/day for critical periods, but would like to see telemetry before it trips.
[05:15] Alex Martinez: noted. let's cover the postmortem doc we circulated - any questions or disagreements?
[05:23] Lisa Chen: one edit - in the doc it says "autoscaler rate-limit" but it's actually a per-account burst cap at the cloud provider level and our op layer honored it. can you soften that wording?
[05:31] Samir Patel: yes i'll update the language to say "account burst cap" and include the provider link.
[05:37] Priya Nair: for mitigations we're listing 5 items in the doc - which of these are immediate vs long-term?
[05:44] Alex Martinez: good question. immediate (within 72 hours): 1) push autoscaler threshold change and queue-depth alerts; 2) share full logs and RCA; 3) update client SDK to support fallback alias. Short-medium term (2 weeks): bench run, dedicated capacity pilot, runbook updates. Long term (1-2 months): system-level regression tests for mixed sequence lengths and more robust fallback routing features.
[06:05] Samir Patel: i'll put owners on each mitigation in the doc.
[06:10] Tom Reynolds: on the dedicated capacity pilot - what's the minimum commitment? we want temporary reserved nodes for two weeks to avoid another outage during our upcoming campaign in march.
[06:20] Alex Martinez: we can do a short pilot: we have 'Dedicated - burst pool' option that can be spun for 2 weeks with a short-term commit; i'll share pricing but likely a short-month pro-rated cost. it's not the full reserved capacity contract; it's more like a 'timeboxed dedicated pool'.
[06:36] Lisa Chen: please send the SKU and the expected throughput.
[06:41] Alex Martinez: yes will do.
[06:44] Priya Nair: about telemetry: can we get per-model token-level cost and per-request KV hit rate? our billing team needs to tie this to the incident cost.
[06:54] Samir Patel: we can provide KV hit/miss metrics and token counts per route; token-level cost is in console and we can export a report. i'll attach those logs.
[07:05] Priya Nair: great. one more: the RCA mentions 'fallback policy didn't match because of variant tags' - can you explain what that means in plain english?
[07:14] Samir Patel: sure. our rollouts use tags like 'primary-v1' vs 'primary-fast' vs 'dedicated-large' and the fallback policy compares tags to see if variants are compatible. because some of your routes explicitly requested primary-v1, the policy refused to route to primary-fast even though it would have been safe. we need a more flexible compatibility matcher that considers architecture instead of exact tag equality.
[07:39] Tom Reynolds: ok makes sense. we will change SDK to use a fallback alias that maps to a set of compatible tags.
[07:47] Alex Martinez: moving on to ops changes: Samir will add a regression test to the eval harness to simulate mixed sequence lengths, and Priya will run the bench that Samir provides. Any blockers?
[07:57] Priya Nair: none expected, we just need the test scripts and a time window.
[08:03] Samir Patel: i'll push the scripts to the shared repo and link in the doc.
[08:07] Lisa Chen: what about audit logs and compliance? our security team asked that any change that touches telemetry is logged - did the hotfix change any telemetry retention or access controls?
[08:17] Samir Patel: no retention changes. the hotfix was runtime-only. all telemetry access is unchanged; we will, however, include a log bundle for your security review.
[08:27] Tom Reynolds: if you can provide a signed attestation or SOC2 artifact referencing this change, that helps.
[08:32] Alex Martinez: we can include the relevant SOC2 controls and pointer to the change log. samir will compile the artifact.
[08:39] Priya Nair: ok next steps and owners?
[08:43] Alex Martinez: recap: Alex to share final RCA, logs, and pricing for temp dedicated pool; Samir to push autoscaler thresholds, alert rules, and bench scripts; Priya to run bench and share results; Tom to evaluate budget for temporary capacity; Lisa to provide critical model list. Follow-up meeting in two weeks.
[09:05] Lisa Chen: sounds good. also please call out the risk matrix in the doc - risk vs impact for long-sequence workloads.
[09:12] Samir Patel: will do.
[09:15] Priya Nair: one small ask - can we get an SLA addendum that says Redwood will notify us within 5 minutes of a cluster-level degradation?
[09:24] Alex Martinez: i can't commit to legal SLA changes on this call but i'll get the account team involved and we can discuss an addendum.
[09:31] Tom Reynolds: thanks all. good to see a clear action plan.
[09:36] Alex Martinez: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and schedule the bench. meeting adjourned.
